outputs.L1:
(CNN) — Efraim Diveroli’s father had hoped his son would become a doctor or lawyer. Instead, Diveroli, 22, is an international arms dealer who, according to his grandfather, is fulfilling his “patriotic” duty.

Diveroli now faces a congressional inquiry over allegations that he sold aging Chinese ammunition to the U.S. military for use in equipping allies in Afghanistan.

He is the president of AEY Inc., a South Florida company that, according to U.S. government documents, has conducted more than $10 million in business with the federal government since 2004. Those documents also show that the company achieved a major breakthrough in 2007, securing contracts worth more than $200 million to supply ammunition, assault rifles, and other weapons to the Afghan National Army and police.

The company’s contract stated that the ammunition would be sourced from Hungary. However, Army investigators found that some of the ammunition supplied to the Afghan military was corroded and had been manufactured in China as long as 46 years earlier.

The New York Times reported Thursday that AEY sought stockpiles and ammunition dumps across former Soviet bloc allies, from Albania to Kazakhstan. Albania was a major customer of Chinese armaments during the 1960s and 1970s, the Times reported.

Angelo Diveroli, Efraim’s grandfather, told CNN affiliate WPLG-TV that his grandson is being targeted by “jealous competitors” in the international arms market. Since childhood, Angelo Diveroli said, Efraim had been deeply familiar with weapons.

“He’s a genius about anything to do with weapons,” the 72-year-old said. “Ever since he was a little boy, I would take him to gun shows and he could identify every model of guns. People would ask: How can he do that so young? He has a gift, I would tell them.”

Michael Diveroli, Efraim’s father, told CNN affiliate WFOR-TV that he wished his son had directed his intellect elsewhere. He described Efraim as “a boy genius” who is “hard to control.”

“I would prefer he became a nice Jewish doctor or lawyer rather than an arms dealer,” WFOR quoted Michael Diveroli as saying.

Yet his son appears to have had a clear sense of the circles in which he was operating. “What goes on in the Albanian Defense Ministry,” The New York Times quoted him as saying. “Who’s clean? Who’s dirty? Don’t want to know about it.”

On a MySpace page last updated in 2005, Diveroli wrote, “I probably grew up way to (sic) fast.” In a glimpse of where the then-19-year-old’s future was heading, he added, “I definately (sic) have the desire to be very successful in my business and this does take up alot (sic) of my time.”

The page also suggests an appetite for excitement. “I’m one of those guys who needs to be entertained and having lots of fun all the time so if your (sic) also an undiagnosed case of ADD look me up,” it said. He listed the weapon-heavy films *Heat* and *Scarface* among his favorites.

A CNN search of Diveroli’s Florida criminal record shows arrests, but no convictions, on offenses ranging from misdemeanor battery to felony possession of stolen property. He has yet to appear in court on a March 3 arrest for driving under the influence.

For now, relatives say Diveroli is out of the country. CNN’s attempts to contact him have been unsuccessful. His grandfather told WPLG that Diveroli is now in Turkey or Albania, carrying out his “patriotic” duty.

“He’s all over the world getting what the military needs,” Angelo Diveroli said.

However, in a MySpace message exchange with *Radar* magazine, a person believed to be David Packouz, a 25-year-old who was AEY’s vice president, referred to Diveroli as “my former scumbag partner” and said he was motivated by money.

“Efraim Diveroli has a serious psychological illness called ‘extreme greed,’” *Radar* quoted him as writing in a report on its Web site.

Packouz declined to discuss AEY with CNN on Friday, saying he had no comment “because of the ongoing investigation.”

# Congress probes AEY Inc. over Afghan ammunition deal and Chinese arms stockpiles

**By Staff Report**

A congressional inquiry into a tiny Miami Beach defense contractor has put a spotlight on how a company run by a young arms dealer, Efraim Diveroli, won hundreds of millions of dollars in U.S. government contracts to supply ammunition to American-backed forces in Afghanistan — and how some of that ammunition allegedly came from decades-old Chinese stockpiles stored in Albania.

The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee examined AEY Inc. after reports and government records raised questions about whether the company provided the Pentagon with ammunition that violated U.S. restrictions on Chinese-made arms. The case became a symbol of the Bush-era wartime contracting boom, in which small private firms could win major deals to supply equipment for conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan.

## Afghan contracts at center of inquiry

AEY Inc., led by Diveroli, was awarded a large Pentagon contract to provide ammunition to the Afghan National Army and Afghan police forces. The contract was intended to help arm U.S.-supported Afghan security units as Washington sought to build local forces capable of fighting the Taliban and other insurgent groups.

But congressional investigators focused on whether AEY misrepresented the origin and condition of the ammunition it supplied. The key concern: U.S. law and procurement rules barred the use of Chinese-made ammunition in such contracts, due to longstanding restrictions on Chinese arms imports.

According to court filings and congressional materials, AEY obtained large quantities of surplus ammunition from Albania, where aging military stockpiles included Chinese-manufactured rounds dating back decades. Investigators looked into whether the ammunition was repackaged to conceal Chinese markings before being shipped to Afghanistan.

The ammunition reportedly included rifle and machine-gun rounds used by Afghan security forces, much of it from Cold War-era stockpiles.

## Albania and Chinese arms stockpiles

Albania played a central role in the controversy. After the fall of its communist government, the country was left with extensive military stockpiles, including ammunition acquired from China during earlier decades.

AEY’s supply chain involved Albanian ammunition depots and intermediaries who helped move the rounds into the U.S. military pipeline. Congressional investigators scrutinized whether crates of ammunition were opened and repacked into different packaging to obscure their Chinese origin.

The inquiry raised broader questions about oversight: how a relatively small company with limited infrastructure was able to win a major defense contract, and whether federal contracting officials adequately vetted AEY’s capacity, suppliers and compliance history before awarding the deal.

## Diveroli’s age and background drew attention

Diveroli’s youth became a major part of the story. He was in his early 20s when AEY secured the Afghan ammunition contract, an extraordinary rise for someone operating from a small office in South Florida.

The inquiry also examined AEY’s business practices and Diveroli’s background, including prior legal issues that had been reported in public records and media accounts. Those records added to concerns among lawmakers about whether the government had done enough due diligence before placing a critical wartime supply contract in the company’s hands.

Diveroli’s online presence also came under scrutiny. A MySpace profile associated with him, widely cited in coverage at the time, portrayed a brash young man fascinated by weapons, wealth and the arms trade. To critics, the profile reinforced concerns that the Pentagon had entrusted a sensitive wartime supply mission to a contractor whose maturity and judgment were open to question.

## Family reactions

Diveroli’s family, according to accounts published during the controversy, reacted with a mix of concern, frustration and defensiveness as the case exploded into national headlines.

Relatives described him as ambitious and unusually interested in the arms business from a young age. Some family members were reportedly alarmed by the scale of the federal investigation and the intense media focus, while others pushed back against the portrayal of Diveroli as simply reckless, arguing that he had entered a complex and competitive contracting world in which larger players also sought profit from war-zone supply deals.

The family’s reaction underscored one of the more unusual elements of the case: a young Miami Beach businessman, still barely older than a college student, had become a central figure in a congressional inquiry involving international arms shipments, U.S. military procurement and the war in Afghanistan.

## David Packouz’s role and comments

David Packouz, who worked with Diveroli at AEY, also became a key figure in public accounts of the company’s rise and fall. Packouz has described the operation as fast-moving, improvised and far larger in consequence than its small staff might suggest.

In later interviews and public comments, Packouz acknowledged that AEY was built around finding low-cost surplus weapons and ammunition overseas and reselling them through U.S. government contracts. He has also said the company’s young employees were operating in an opaque international arms market where paperwork, brokers and supply-chain claims were central to getting deals done.

Packouz ultimately faced legal consequences in connection with the case, as did Diveroli. Both men became widely known after the episode was later dramatized in popular culture, though the congressional inquiry and court records laid out a more serious picture: a wartime contracting scandal involving ammunition destined for U.S.-allied forces in an active conflict zone.

## Criminal case followed inquiry

The congressional scrutiny was followed by federal criminal proceedings. Prosecutors accused AEY and its principals of defrauding the U.S. government by misrepresenting the origin of ammunition supplied under the Afghan contract.

Diveroli later pleaded guilty in connection with the case and was sentenced to prison. The case became one of the most prominent examples of misconduct in wartime contracting, highlighting weaknesses in procurement oversight and the risks of relying on private brokers to source arms from unstable or poorly monitored foreign stockpiles.

## Larger questions for the Pentagon

For lawmakers, the AEY case was never just about one contractor. It raised systemic questions about how the Pentagon awarded contracts during wartime, how it monitored subcontractors and foreign suppliers, and how ammunition with prohibited origins could enter a U.S.-funded supply chain.

The inquiry also exposed the uneasy reality of the global surplus arms market: weapons and ammunition manufactured decades earlier can move through layers of brokers, storage depots and shell companies before arriving on a battlefield.

In the AEY case, those rounds were meant for Afghan soldiers and police fighting alongside U.S. forces. Instead, they became evidence in a political and criminal controversy over whether America’s rush to arm its allies had outpaced its ability to police the contractors doing the work.
